stem: When reviewing Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) epidemiology during evaluation, which incidence pattern aligns with standard references?

options.text: Reactivation infections occur in approximately 30% to 40% of EBV-seropositive recipients
Reactivation never occurs in EBV-seropositive transplant recipients
Reactivation occurs in fewer than 5% of all seropositive recipients
EBV reactivation applies only to kidney recipients

explanation.rationale_correct: Reactivation Epstein-Barr virus infections occur in approximately 30% to 40% of EBV-seropositive recipients, whereas primary infection occurs in most seronegative recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Reactivation is common in seropositive recipients rather than absent.
rationale_incorrect.C: The referenced reactivation rate is substantially higher than 5%.
rationale_incorrect.D: EBV reactivation is described across solid-organ transplant recipients rather than kidney recipients alone.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Epstein-Barr virus → 2. Incidence
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Reactivation infections occur in approximately 30% to 40% of EBV-seropositive recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Epstein-Barr virus → 2.b. (reactivation in 30–40% of EBV-seropositive recipients); PDF p. 198 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. EBV-reactivation incidence angle distinct from primary-infection incidence (cctc-2110) and replication rates with antilymphocyte therapy; anchor verified on Cupples p. 198.

stem: A transplant candidate treated with antithymocyte globulin asks about Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) replication risk after transplant. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: EBV replication occurs in about 80% of recipients who receive antilymphocyte antibody therapy
Antilymphocyte therapy eliminates all EBV replication risk
EBV replication never occurs after transplantation
EBV replication risk is identical whether or not antilymphocyte therapy is used

explanation.rationale_correct: Epstein-Barr virus replication occurs in approximately 20% to 30% of all solid-organ transplant recipients and in about 80% of recipients who receive antilymphocyte antibody therapy.

rationale_incorrect.B: Antilymphocyte therapy is associated with higher EBV replication rates rather than eliminating risk.
rationale_incorrect.C: EBV replication is common after transplantation, especially with potent immunosuppression.
rationale_incorrect.D: Replication rates are higher with antilymphocyte antibody therapy than in the overall recipient population.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Epstein-Barr virus → 2. Incidence
primary_anchor.quote_hint: EBV replication occurs in approximately 20% to 30% of all solid organ transplant recipients and in 80% of recipients who receive antilymphocyte antibody therapy

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Epstein-Barr virus → 2.a. (EBV replication in ~80% with antilymphocyte antibody therapy); PDF p. 198 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. EBV-replication rate with antilymphocyte therapy distinct from reactivation incidence (cctc-2125) and potent-immunosuppression PTLD risk (cctc-2114); anchor verified on Cupples p. 198.

stem: During pretransplant sexual-health teaching, which contraception guidance aligns with standard references?

options.text: Emergency contraception may be considered in certain circumstances
Emergency contraception is contraindicated in all transplant candidates and recipients
Emergency contraception is the only method ever discussed
Contraception counseling applies only after ten years post-transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Sexual health teaching includes that emergency contraception may be considered in certain circumstances along with other contraceptive and pregnancy-planning counseling.

rationale_incorrect.B: Emergency contraception may be considered rather than being universally contraindicated.
rationale_incorrect.C: Multiple contraceptive options are discussed rather than emergency contraception alone.
rationale_incorrect.D: Contraception counseling is part of ongoing sexual health teaching rather than being deferred for a decade.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → k. Sexual health → v.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Emergency contraception may be considered in certain circumstances

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → k. Sexual health → v. (emergency contraception may be considered in certain circumstances); PDF p. 121 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Emergency-contraception angle distinct from IUD counseling (cctc-1126) and oral-contraception thromboembolic risk (cctc-1123); anchor verified on Cupples p. 121.

stem: When counseling about posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD) risk in pediatric and older recipients, which age-related factor aligns with standard references?

options.text: Young infants and children and older age recipients are at increased PTLD risk
Age has no relationship to PTLD risk
Only recipients aged 30 to 40 years are at PTLD risk
Pediatric recipients have zero PTLD risk compared with adults

explanation.rationale_correct: Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease risk factors include age at both extremes: young infants and young children and older age recipients.

rationale_incorrect.B: Age is listed among PTLD risk factors.
rationale_incorrect.C: Young pediatric and older recipients are specifically identified rather than only middle-aged adults.
rationale_incorrect.D: Pediatric recipients, especially young infants and children, have increased PTLD risk rather than zero risk.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Epstein-Barr virus → 3. Risk factors for PTLD
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Age: young (infants and young children) and older age recipients

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Epstein-Barr virus → 3.h. (young infants/children and older age as PTLD risk factors); PDF p. 198 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Twenty-sixth pediatric recipient in bank; PTLD age-risk angle distinct from pediatric acetaminophen fever guidance (cctc-1096) and pediatric bacterial-infection combo (cctc-1097); anchor verified on Cupples p. 198.
